en: Salutations to the illustrious Sundaragaṇapati. [The Thousand Names of Śiva] [The Hymn of the Thousand Names of Mṛtyuñjaya]. (,,,,,,,,)
The Thousand-Name Hymn of Śiva (Śivasahasranāmastotra) Hari said: Oṃ. How did the one known as the Sage (Ṛṣi) obtain the discus called Sudarśana? How did Hari [obtain it]?
O Mahādeva, O Bhagavat, it behoves you to speak of the son of [Bhava];
the illustrious son became the lord of the gods and asuras. [He was] equal to... the seer of all beings. And the gods, having been defeated by the Daityas, [sought] Viṣṇu.
Having arrived at the place of sacrifice,
they were all terrified with fear; seeing them wounded, distressed, and groaning, the Blessed One Janārdana, the God of gods, spoke to Rudra.
(6th line) "O gods, for what purpose have you come? Having heard these words, which grant a boon, the gods took them away.
(7th line) Having bowed down, they said to the Lord:
"O Lord of all, we have come here to you for refuge; you alone are the destination for those who are burning with the forest fire of saṃsāra. You are the Supreme Person and our protector;
therefore, you ought to slay them quickly."
Desiring their own prosperity and longing for battle, he took up [the weapon] for the sake of slaying Jalandhara from the hand of the Trident-bearer.
"O one of great strength, perform the slaughter of those Daityas! Having heard those words of theirs, the Blessed One—
Having informed the gods, "I shall thus create a son," the illustrious Śaṅkara went to the Himavat mountain and performed worship.
Having installed the *liṅga* there, having performed the bath with pure, auspicious waters, and having worshipped Śaṅkara with devotion by means of the *rudra* [mantra],
then—
He praised the Supreme Lord with the Thousand Names (*Nāmasahasra*), and having worshipped him with a thousand lotuses, Keśava worshipped the highly fortunate Bhavānī with names that inspire joy.
[Of this *Śrī Śiva-sahasra*...]
Of this great mantra of the *Nāmastotra*, Nārada is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandas*), and the Supreme Self, Śrī Sadāśiva, is the deity (*devatā*).

"Bhavaḥ Śiva-haro-ri-dim" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); "sarvatattvāvalambana" is the power (*śakti*); and "gāyatrīvallabhaḥ prāṃśuḥ" is the peg (*kīlaka*). [This is employed] for the sake of attaining the grace of Śrī Sadāśiva, which is unsurpassed and uninterrupted.

The application for the recitation (*japa-viniyoga*): To Bhava, whose body is smeared with ashes, the self of cessation (*nivṛtti-ātman*), [I offer] *namaḥ* to the heart. Oṃ Khaṃ! To the one possessing the bow of Dharma and Wisdom, to the one of great energy, [I offer] *svāhā* to the head. Oṃ Maṃ! To the one of great strength, the lord of sacrifice, the sacrificer, the limb of knowledge (*jñānāṅga*), [I offer] *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Oṃ Śiṃ...

To the one whose vehicle is sacrifice, who has a thousand heads, a thousand arms, and wears armor—*hūṃ*. *Oṃ vaṃ*, to the Lord of All, the Three-Eyed One, the Destroyer of Cities, who possesses three eyes—*vauṣaṭ*. *Oṃ yaṃ*, to the one with the broken axe, the Swift, who is affectionate toward those who take refuge, and who is the support of all principles—*phaṭ*. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ*.
The meditation on the boundary of the directions:
[one should visualize] him who resembles ten million suns and has three eyes.
Adorned with ornaments, bearing a trident, sword, mace, discus, spear, and noose, the omnipresent Lord, with hands granting boons and fearlessness,
and decorated with all manner of jewelry— thus did Viṣṇu, endowed with faith and devotion, meditate upon Śiva.
The root is Śiva, the destroyer of existence, who is abundant, possessed of two eyes, the foremost in virtuous conduct, and the Great Lord Śarva-Śambhu.
The Lord of the World, the Immovable One, the Ruler, the Thousand-eyed, the Lord of Creatures, the Most Excellent, the Bestower of Boons,
the Commander, the Auspicious One, the Supreme Lord, the Bearer of the Gaṅgā, the Wielder of the Trident, the Supreme...
He whose sole purpose is the welfare of beings, the omniscient one, who bears matted hair and a mountain-bow along with all the gods and others;
he whose crest is the moon, the wise one who wears the moon upon his head, the lord of all immortals, the essence of the Vedāntas, the possessor of the skull-bowl (kapālin).
Nilalohita;
he who is above and below the stages of meditation (dhyāna); the Lord of Ganas worshipped by yogis; the eight-formed one (aṣṭamūrti);
the one whose form is the universe; the speaker of [the truth]; the means for attaining heaven.
He who is attainable through knowledge, possessed of firm wisdom, the God of gods, the three-eyed one, Vāmadeva, Mahādeva, the Lord, the all-pervading, the leaf-like,
the one whose form is the universe, and the multiformed.
The Lord of Speech, belonging to the lunar fortnight, most pure, in harmony with all means of valid cognition, bull-bannered, having the bull as his vehicle;
(3rd line) the Lord who wields the Pināka bow and the Khaṭvāṅga staff, of variegated attire, eternal, consisting of mind; (4th line) the Mind-made One.
The Great Yogin, the Firm One, the Cosmic Egg, Dhūrjaṭi; the Death of Death,
the Skirted One (Kṛttivāsas), the Auspicious One, the Praṇava, the One with the Serpent Crest (Nāgacūḍa), the One with Beautiful Eyes, Dūrvāsas, and the Subduer of Cities (Puraśāsana).
The teacher of the deer [is] devoted to the Supreme Lord, the beginningless, middleless, and endless Giriśa, the kinsman of... (6th line) ... (7th line).
Ku...rabandhu Śrīkaṇṭha, the best among those praised by the world, the deer-marked one, the deity of the Sāmaveda, the wielder of the bow, the blue-throated one,
the bearer of the axe, the large-eyed one, the hunter of deer, the arrow-wielder.
The Blessed One, who subdues those who speak ill, whose abode is the Dharma, who is the field of patience, the bearer of the eye of fortune,
the fierce Lord of Creatures, the protector of the Tākṣas, who speaks kindly to his beloved devotees, who is self-controlled, a source of compassion, and skillful.
Kapardin, the subduer of Kama;
whose abode is the cremation ground, the three-eyed one, Maheśvara who dwells in the cremation ground;
the witness of the world's actions, the lord of the elements, the master of all deeds, and the great medicinal herbs.
The supreme protector and guardian,
accessible through knowledge, ancient, pure in soul through right conduct and excellent policy, he is Soma, more cooling than the moon, and blissful.
Soma, Amṛtapas, Samyoma, Mahānīti, Mahāmati, Ajātaśatru, Āloka, Sambhāvya, Havyavāhana,
Lokakāra, Vedakāra, Sūtrakāra, Sanātana, and Maharṣi.
Kapilācārya, Viśvadīpti, Vilocana;
Pinākapāṇi, Bhūdeva, Svastida, Svastri;
Kṛtsna, Sudhī, Dhātrīdhāmakara, Sarva, Sarvajña, and Sarvagocara.

The creator of Brahmā, the creator of the universe, the beloved of the Kaṇikāra tree, the poet, the one with branches, the one with many branches, the one whose branches are cows, Śiva, and the supreme physician.
Gangāplava, Umaka, Bhavya, Puṣkarasthapati, Sthira, Vijitātman, Avidheyātman, Bhūtavāhana,
Sāradhī, Sagaṇa, Gaṇakāra, Sukīrti, and Chinnasaṃśaya— [these are] Kāma...

The Lord, whose body is smeared with ashes and covered in dust, who loves ashes and sleeps upon them, the beloved of Kāma, who has brought the scriptures under his control, who is surrounded by those who have turned away from the world, and who is eternally Śiva, having forever dispelled the mass of unrighteousness; ||| (f3.a, 1st line) ||| [he is] the God Kāmapāla.
Stainless, four-armed, clothed in all-encompassing garments, difficult to approach, hard to attain, and impenetrable, he is skilled in all weapons;
[he is] the supreme self.
Yoginilaya, Sūtantu, Tantuvardhana, Śubhāṅga, Yogasāraṅga, Ojagadīśa, Janārdana,
Bhasmaśuddhikara, Merurojasvin, and Śuddhavi...
The planet, the one with golden seed, the youthful, the abode of rays, the refuge of greatness;
the great heart, the great path, he who is saluted by hosts of Siddhas and Vidyādharas; the wearer of the tiger skin, the great being of the serpent.
The great sage;
the embodiment of truth of the nectar-rayed moon; the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice; the wind; the knower of the twenty-five principles; and the one who is devoted to the Pārijāta tree.
Easily accessible, well-conducted, the son of Śūna, the sole abode of Vāmya, a treasure-trove,

the preceptor of the castes and stages of life, the vanquisher of the enemy of the castes, the scorcher of those who pierce [the truth], emaciated by the destruction of the hermitages, possessed of knowledge, and immovable.
He who is unshakable, the embodiment of valid authority, difficult to comprehend, of excellent complexion, and whose vehicle is the wind; who holds the bow,
who is the ocean of the science of archery, a mass of virtues, a mine of qualities, possessed of infinite vision, and bliss itself.
Having subdued the senses and conquered pride, he of massive body bows down; he is an expert in all crafts,
free from passion, self-disciplined, devoted to austerity, and has the spirits as his vehicle.
One whose dress is disarrayed, who has conquered desire, who is dear to people, whose nature is auspicious, who is well-disposed, the lord of all the world’s creatures,
an ascetic, and a savior.
The wise one, the preeminent and imperishable Lord, whose inner self resides within the hearts of the world-protectors, whose eyes behold the lotus at the beginning of the kalpa;
he who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the scriptures, who is the refuge of vows and restraints, and who is Rāhu, Sūrya, Śani, Ketu, Virāma, and coral.

He whose skin is radiant, who is accessible through devotion, who is the Supreme Brahman, the deer-marked one (the moon), the arrow, the merchant, the sinless one, the mountain, the abode of the gods,
the constellation Svāti, the Supreme Self, and the Lord of the Universe.
The abode of all actions, the auspicious one who bestows auspiciousness, the great ascetic, the long-ascetic, the most steadfast, the most heroic,
the eternal, the day, and the year.
The scorcher of foes declared him to be the supreme authority, the mantra that creates the year, the means of realization, and the all-seeing one;
he is the unborn, the Lord of all, the perfected one, possessing great seed and great strength, the one fit for yoga, the Great God, the perfected one, the mountain of all, and the infallible.
Vasu, Vasumān, Satya, the remover of all sins, Hara, the immortal, the eternal, the peaceful, the one with arrows in hand, the majestic,
the bearer of the water-pot, the archer, the Vedāṅga, and the Veda.
The sage of the *vit* syllable, the eater of radiant food, the one who is difficult to approach for the eyes of the world,
beyond the senses of Indra, the great illusionist, the abode of all, the four-footed, the great yogi of the yoga of time, the great [light].
He possessed the strength of a hawk,
was of great intellect and great heroism, and was the destroyer of the cities of his enemies; he was a night-stalker who moved among the *pretas*, possessed great power, and was of great splendor.
Possessing a splendor of form that is beyond description,
with a gait that is helpful to all, one who has heard much, who is full of sweetness, whose self is disciplined, and who shines with innate luster.
He who bears vigor, splendor, and brilliance; the dancer; he who is desired by all; the lover of the fragments of the Vedas;
whose nature is eternal light; the powerful one;
the mantra of clear syllables; the prosperity; the battle; and the autumnal cloud.
The creator of the beginning of the Yugas, the one whose path is the turning of the wheel, the profound, the bull-vehicled;
the beloved, the most distinguished among the distinguished, the desired;
the Śarabha, whose vehicle is the Śarabha; the ocean of waters, the presiding lord, the victorious, the conqueror, the protector.
Hari, whose golden armor is established by the measure of [his] splendor, is the liberator of the hosts of gods; he is the science of the wise and the glory of the enlightened.
He is the form of the *sāla* tree, the one who measures, the cutter, the one whose cave is impenetrable;
he is the doer of instruments, the cause, and the non-doer, the liberator of all who are bound; he is resolve, the established order, the giver of stations, and the support of the world.
The twice-born Dundubhīlalita, whose self is the source of the universe, abides within the Self;
he is the Lord of the Universe, Virabhadra,
the Ordainer of the Virāsana posture, the Sovereign, the crest-jewel of heroes, the one beyond speech, the ocean of bliss, and the upholder of the mountain.
The bearer of commands, the egg of the trident, Śipiviṣṭa, the refuge of Śiva, Bālakhilya, the one of great conduct,
the sharp-rayed, the solitary, and the sky-goer.

Delightful, a worthy refuge, possessing excellent *brahman*-nature, a lord of the earth, bountiful, of the Kauśika lineage, rich in cattle, radiant, and the accomplisher of all goals—[he is] Lalā... (5th line) ... (6th line).
Ṭākṣa, Viśvadeva, Sāra, Samsāracakrabhṛt, Amoghadaṇḍa, Madhyastha, Hiraṇya, Brahmavarcasī,
Paramārya, Parapada, Śambara, Vyāghra, and Anala.
Ruci, Vararuci, Vādya, Vācaspati, Ahaspati, Ravi, Virocana, Skanda, Śāstṛ,
Vaivasvata, Arjuna, Yukti, Unnatakīrti, Śāntarāga, and Purañjaya.

(3rd line) The dweller on Kailāsa, whose eyes are the sun and moon, who removes the fear of the darkness of ignorance, and whose activity is unimpeded; (4th line) [He is] the one whose work is never obstructed.
He is eternal, eternally auspicious, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious;
his fame resounds afar, he is the brother of the universe, the object of meditation, and the destroyer of dreams.
The destroyer of the evil deeds of the enemies of the stars, the one who causes great joy, the unbearable one, the source of fear, the beginningless one, the lord of the earth,
the one whose crown is the goddess Lakṣmī,
the protector of the gods, the protector of the universe, the one beloved by the universe, the heroic one, and the beautiful one.
Gada, Janaka, Janajana, Janmādi, Pritimān, Nitimān, Dṛḍha;
Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, Bhānu, Bhīma, Abhimaparākrama, Praṇava, Satpathācāra, Mahākāya, Mahā...
Dhana; Janmādhipa; Mahādeva, who has reached the further shore of all scriptures; Tattvavit (the knower of reality); Ekātman (the one self); Vibhūti; and Bhūtibhūṣaṇa (adorned with ashes).

The Lord of birth, death, and old age, who is the seer, the Brāhmaṇa, the Knower, and Viṣṇu; he is the sacrifice, the Lord of sacrifice, the sacrificer, and the one whose prowess makes the fruit of sacrifice non-vain.

He who is the great mountain difficult to bear, the sacrificial army, the limb of the sacrifice, and the vehicle of the sacrifice; he from whom the five Brahmans are produced, the source of all, the stainless one...
he who is self-born, without beginning or end, the thirty-sixth, and the universal soul.
Lokadhṛk, Gāyatrivallabha, Prāṃśu, Viśvāvāsa, Prabhākara, Śuci, Garīyān,
Bhara, Sammṛḍ, Suṣeṇa, Suraśatruhā, Amogha, Ariṣṭamardana, Mukunda, and Vikata.
Jvara is self-luminous, following light, and having the Self as his light; he is immovable, tawny,
with reddish-brown hair and beard, with eyes like weapons, and possesses a body of triple intelligence.
The great sage Jñānaskanda, whose form is a flood of light arising from supreme knowledge; the sun of the sky [of the mind], the teacher of yoga, the lord of the day—
sublime.

He whose fame consists of the assembly of the industrious and the assembly of the perfected yogis; who rests upon the sixfold Svādhiṣṭhāna, the Lord of Serpents garlanded with stars; whose movement is through the sky of Maṇipūra, the city of jewels that purifies the six senses and destroys sin; [residing] in the lotus of the heart.
The abode, the parrot, the hawk, Vṛṣākapi;

the satisfied lord of the planets, Kṛṣṇa, the one with wealth, the destroyer of pride (or the destroyer of [the demon] Naṭha); the enemy of unrighteousness, the imperishable, the much-invoked, the much-praised.
The womb of Brahman, the vast womb, the source of the cause of Dharma, the traditional scripture; the Sugata who desires the welfare of the world, the Youth, the arrival of virtue.
Golden-hued, consisting of light, having approached [the world], the remover of darkness, free from disease, the sun-like one,
the lord of the twice-born Viśvāmitra,
the light of Brahman— may he grant us excellent awakening.
The supreme light, Mātāmaha, Mātariśvan, Manasvin, Nāgahāradhṛk,
Pulastya, Pulaha, Agastya, Jātakarṇa, Parāśara, and Viriñci, whose wisdom is free from all veils.
Viṣṭaraśravas, self-born, the embodiment of self-knowledge, of great renown, the crest-jewel of the world, Viraja,
and Satyaparākrama.
Vyālakalpa, Mahākalpa, Kalpavṛkṣa, Kalādharā,
Alaṅkariṣṇu, Acala, Rociṣmān, Vikrama, Krama, Aśva.
Ptapadī, Gīpavana, Śikhisāradhi, Asammṛṣṭotidhi, Śukra,
Pramādipādapāśana, Vasuśravas, Kavyavāha, Pratapta, and Viśvabhoja.
Jana, Jaya, Jarāri, Śamana, Lohitāśva, Uṣṭra, Navāt,
Vṛṣadaśva, Nabhasya, Nara, Supratīka, Tamisrahā, Nidāgha, Tapana, Meghapakṣa, Parapura.
Jaya, Sukhānila, Saniṣpanna, Surabhi, Śiśirātmaka, Vasanta, Mādhava, Grīṣma,
Nabhasya, and Bījavāhana.
The intellect of the mind, the ego, the knower of the field, the protector of the field, the one born from fire, the ocean, the ripening [of karma], the creator of the universe—
this is to be known as the Unspoken, the Supreme.
The abode of ultimate bliss, the mountain, the destroyer of the hosts of Nāgas, Dhanus, Dhāris, and Dānavas,
the subduer of enemies, the progenitor of Cāmuṇḍī, the enemy, the one free from thorns, the remover of the world's thorns, the four Vedas, the four-armed one.
He is clever, handsome, and pleasing to behold; he is the deity of the Vedas, the one praised by the Vedas, and the abode of the auspicious Lord Śiva.
He is the embodiment of sacrifice, the one of great form, the one who takes all forms, and that which is both moving and unmoving.
The sustainer of logic, the source of the path of reasoning, the stainless one, the thousand-headed Lord of Gods, the destroyer of all enemies.
Mu...
The staff-bearer, the deformed, the one of wondrous form, the one subdued by the staff, the preeminent in virtues, the tawny-eyed,
the one with a horse-like neck, the wind-necked, the free from disease,
the thousand-armed, and the Lord of All.
The forest-dweller, the sustainer of all worlds, the one seated upon the lotus, the supreme light who bestows the fruit of the higher and the lower;
the one born from the lotus, the great womb, the womb of the universe, the far-sighted, the knower of the higher and the lower, the giver of boons.
The Supreme Lord is exceedingly powerful;
he is the teacher of gods and asuras, and is repeatedly saluted by gods, asuras, and men.
He is the great mantra of gods and asuras, and the great refuge of gods and asuras.
The God of gods, the bestower of boons upon gods, sages, and asuras; the Lord of gods and asuras, the divine Great Lord of gods and asuras.
He who consists of all the gods, the inconceivable one, born from the self of the deity; he whose head is presided over by Indra, the tiger among gods, the joy of the gods, the sun;
the foremost leader of the wise, the best of all the gods.
The supreme dispeller of darkness, devoted to meditation on Śiva, the illustrious Śikhaṇḍin, beloved of Pārvatī;
(line 5) wielder of the thunderbolt, the firm supporter, the slayer of Narasiṃha, the celibate wanderer through the worlds; (line 6)
The lord of wealth for those who practice the Dharma;

Nandin and Nandīśvara; the destroyer of poverty; the wearer of matted hair; the pure one; the presiding deity of the *liṅga*; the presiding deity of the gods; the presiding deity of the ages (*yuga*); and the bringer of the ages.

He who bestows heaven by his own will, whose voice consists of the beautiful sounds of heaven, the overseer of the seed, the creator of the seed, the performer of dharma, and the increaser of dharma; he who is guile, great guile, and supreme guile, the Great Lord of all beings, and the presiding lord of the abode in the cremation ground.
His form is like a snare;
his light clearly illuminates the other worlds; he is compassionate toward his devotees; he is the one who struck down the enemy of the gods, the slayer of Andhaka, who fell from the neck of Viṣṇu.
He who has cast off defects, the destroyer of the senses, the one possessing the teeth of Pūṣan, Dhūrjaṭi, the wielder of the broken axe, the manifest, the partless, and the sinless.

Ana...raḥ, the support of the arts (kalādhāraḥ), the follower of Pāṇḍara-gomṛḍa, one whose merit is sought by the full [moon], Sukra...locana, fond of the singing of the Sāmaveda, and cruel. Puṇya... (f10.b, 1st line).

The embodiment of health, the one who bestows the fruit of swift speed, the matted-haired one, the Lord of Life, the ender of life, the one who destroys [suffering], the giver of wealth, the refuge of the virtuous, the one worthy of honor, the peaceful one, the one with black ears, and the one who [bestows]... Ka.
Lādhara;
the venerable Mahākāla; Satbhūti; Sarvarāyaṇa; Candrasañjīvana;
Śastrālokagīta; Marādhipa.
The kinsman of the world, the subduer of the world, the knower of gratitude, adorned with fame, the unfailing, the imperishable, the infinite, and the foremost among all upholders of the scriptures;
(6th line)
Tumburu, Mahāśoka, Viśoka, the destroyer of sorrow; Lord of the three worlds, the soul of the three worlds, pure in intellect, unborn;
characterized by the unmanifest, manifest, and the unmanifest-unmanifest.
The lord of the people, whose form is composed of excellent character and supreme virtues,
who is borne by the earth, who is Viṣṇu, the protector of subjects, the swan, whose gait is like that of a swan, who consists of light, who is formless, and the eater of the world.
Jaṭeśvara is the knower of the Vedas, the creator, the giver, the protector, and the four-faced one;
he dwells upon the peak of Kailāsa and is the true refuge for all beings.
Hiraṇyagarbha, the sky, the Puruṣa, the first-born, the father, the abode of beings, the lord of beings, the bestower of prosperity, and the sovereign of the world.
He who has abandoned the practice of worldly association, who is devoted to Brahman, who is dear to Brāhmaṇas, who is beloved by the gods, who is the protector of the gods,
who knows the divine, who contemplates the divine,
who is liberated from poison, whose eyes are tremulous, and who bears the bull as his emblem.
The increaser of virtue, free from intoxication, free from egoism, free from delusion, and free from hypocrisy;
the primordial sound of the past, future, and present; the source of manifestation, whose wealth is not confusion; who has transcended the three states of existence.
Hākeśa, the sole expert in the affairs of others;
earless, yet filled with joy; guileless, yet the crusher of deceit; truthful, virtuous, and real; he who has made his fame a pillar and whose arrival is like a sacred scripture.

(6th line) One whose collection of virtues is unshakable, who is not of a single nature yet performs manifold deeds, the beloved of Śrī, the auspicious beginning, the one with a gentle gaze, the conqueror of the mind—
(7th line) [he is] Mañjaya.

Dwelling on the earth, the creator of prosperity, terrifying through his splendor, the upholder of prosperity; bodiless, yet the body of the Lord, the great youth possessing the knowledge of all things; established in truth, the great renunciant, and the one whose power is immeasurable.
The ultimate refuge, the bestower of the highest goal and livelihood, the ocean of grammar and sacred revelation,
the fire that consumes the impurities of the wicked, the destroyer of the stains of hypocrisy, he who has cast down his enemies by his own splendor.
The destroyer;
he who possesses a crest-lock, armor, a trident, a flame, a shaven head, earrings, a girdle, a bodice, a garland, and a staff— one whose intellect perceives the essence of saṃsāra.
The Immortal All-Conqueror,
the Lion, the Great Jewel of Massed Splendor, whose self is incalculable and immeasurable, who has destroyed [all obstacles] and is skilled in the body.

The knower of medicine, the one to be known, the protector of the sky, the lord of all gods and sages; he who is free from darkness, difficult to overcome, gentle, and pleasant to behold; the lord of the gods, the refuge, the bestower of happiness, and the goal for all virtuous beings.
He who casts a stain upon those who eat at improper times, who has reduced Vāsuki to a mere grain of dust,
the great archer who is the destroyer of the great elephant-demon, who is free from the fetters of worldly attachment, the jewel of heaven, kindled by the sun, the bestower of perfection— Siddhi.
Sāyana;
Vivṛta, Suvṛta, Śilpin, Vyūḍhoraska, Mahābhuja;
Ekajyotis, Nirātaṅka, and the beloved of Nara-Nārāyaṇa.

Free from worldly attachment, his self is beyond conceptual proliferation; he is the destroyer of agitation and distraction, worthy of praise, fond of hymns, and the praiser himself; he is the pervasive Lord of Speech, undisturbed by confusion.

The method for the stainless path, the mass of knowledge, the sequence [of practice], the manifestation, the destroyer of the petty and the small, the eternally heroic one, the battle... [f. 13a, l. 2]

The destroyer of the three cities, Śākalya, the lord of the night, the supreme teacher, the one whose intellect is all-pervading, the protector of those who take refuge in him, the essence of aesthetic flavor,
the knower of flavors, the knower of the essence, and the knower of all principles.
With support.
May there be auspiciousness. (f13b is blank) (f14a, first line)
O best of the twice-born, having thus praised the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain with a thousand names on the northern pedestal, Puṇḍarīka [praised him] with devotion.

To the one of inexhaustible qualities, to the one who bestows skill, to the one who cleaves the teeth of Pūṣan.
To Dhūrjaṭi, to Khaṇḍaparaśu,
who is without shoulders or neck.
To the one free from conceptual construction, the faultless, and the supportless.
To the one who is the support of all arts,
whose limbs are white,
and who follows Mṛḍa.
To the Full One (the third part), to the Filler, to the Meritorious One.
To the one who delights in the pure, to the one with beautiful eyes,
to the beloved of the singers of the Sāman hymns.
To Kūlarāya,
whose fame is meritorious and who is free from ailment.
To Manojakhāya (the fourth part),
to Trīkarāya,
to Jaṭāla...
Masters of life, bringers of the end of life, for the sake of the infinite.
To the one with golden seed,
the bestower of wealth,
the true refuge.
To Satkṛti, to Śānta,
and to Kālakarṇi.
To Kaladhara, who is to be honored and meditated upon, the Great Time (Mahakala).
To the one who brings about the welfare of the virtuous,
the supreme refuge,
and the moon that restores life.
To the one who is her own, the secret of the world, and the sovereign of the immortals.
To the friend of the world,
the protector of the world, the one who is grateful.
For the sake of one adorned with fame,
for that which is imperishable, for that which is inexhaustible. (Third Part)
To the one who wears the excellent garment of the essence of all teachings, to the ancient one, to the Great Śoka.
To the one free from sorrow,
the destroyer of grief, the Lord of the three worlds.
To Adhokṣaja, the soul of the three worlds, for the sake of pure increase.
To the one whose characteristics are unmanifest, to the unmanifest, and to the manifest-unmanifest.
To the lord of the people,
who possesses excellent character and preeminent virtues.
To the one who has gone to the limbs [of the body], to the bearer of the offerings to the ancestors (Kavyavāhana), to the protector of the worship of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
To the swan,
to the one whose gait is like a swan, to absorption.
To the one consisting of light, formless, the sustainer of the world.
To Jaṭeśvara, to the Veda, to the Ordainer.
To the creator, the giver, the sustainer.
To the four-faced one,
who dwells upon the peak of Kailāsa and resides everywhere.
To Hiraṇyagarbha,
who is the sky for the sake of the attainment of the sixfold state.
To the primordial Person, the Father.
To Bhūttalaya, to Bhūtapati, to Bhūta...
To Bhuvaneśvara,
the united one,
the knower of sacrifice.
To the one who has created Brahman, the foremost, the beloved of the Brāhmaṇas.
To Devapriya,
the supporter of the world, the knower of the Vedas.
For Devacintaka,
for Viṣamukta, for [Vi]lākṣa.
To the one who increases prosperity, to the one who causes prosperity to grow, to the one free from intoxication.
To the one free from egoism, free from delusion, and free from affliction.
To the one who bestows pride upon pride,
the one who is without pride.
To him who has completed many cycles of rebirth,
who has attained perfect mastery,
and who possesses a thousand rays of light.
To the one whose characteristic is the primordial nature of the nose,
the support of the past, future, and present,
and the source of manifestation.
For the destruction of ignorance,
for the sake of the supreme goal, and for the sake of action.
To Mahākeśa,
the sole expert in the affairs of others,
the earless one.
To him who has brought joy, who is sincere, and who crushes all pretense.
To the one who speaks the truth,
to the witness, to Truth itself.
To him who has established the pillar of fame, who has mastered the scriptures, and whose multitude of virtues is unshakable.
To Śrī Vallabha, who is not of a single nature and who performs manifold deeds.
For the auspicious undertaking, for the peaceful and blessed one,
for the accumulation [of merit].
To the one who dwells upon the earth,
the creator of prosperity,
for the sake of well-being.
For the sake of adornment, for the sake of maintaining prosperity, for the bodiless one.
To Bhaktakāyastha,
the knower of time,
the great ascetic.
To the one whose conduct is truth,
who possesses great renunciation, and who has mastered the power of will...
To the one who bestows the boon of acting for the sake of others,
to the one who has divided the ocean of the Vedas,
[and] to the one who perceives virtues even in those who are not his own.
To the one who is stainless, the destroyer of stains, who is auspicious by nature.
To Maṇyastha,
the slayer of enemies, the destroyer of foes.
To Śikhaṇḍin, to the one clad in armor, to the wielder of the trident.
To the one with a topknot, the shaven-headed one, and the one wearing earrings.
To Mekhalin,
Kañcukin, and Mālin.
To the one who possesses speech,
who brings about the essence of saṃsāra, and who is immortal.
To Sarvajit Siṃha, who lies in peace, (the third part).
To the jewel of the Kalāmas,
the incalculable one,
whose nature is immeasurable.
To the physician who is skilled in treatment and proficient in his craft.
To the supreme Lord of Sages, [belonging to the] Gotra...vi...mara-munīśvara.
To the one who is difficult to overcome,
sweet, and pleasant to behold.
To the Lord of the Gods,
the refuge,
the source of bliss.
To the one who is all gods, who is the refuge of the virtuous, and who devours time.
To the one who made Vāsuki his girdle of tinkling bells,
the great archer.
By Mahībhaktreṇa,
for Niṣkalaṅkaya (the second part),
for Sakṛdbalāya.
To Dūmaṇa-taraṇa-dhanya.
To the one who bestows accomplishment, who has perfected the means of attainment, and who is fully revealed.
To the well-rolling artisan,
who is free from disease.
To the one with mighty arms, the protector of the earth, who is free from all affliction.
To the one beloved by Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
who is untainted and whose self is free from conceptual proliferation.
To the one who is free from agitation, to the one worthy of praise, to the one who delights in being praised.
To the one whose body is pervaded by white [light],
who is undisturbed.
To the mass of knowledge, which is the faultless path to liberation.
To the one who is uncontrived, whose mental activity is perfectly tranquil, and who is not petty.
To the destroyer of the wicked,
to the eternally pure, to the foremost leader of the host.
To Yātriśa Śākalya,
the Lord of the Night.
To the Guru of the ultimate truth,
who has increased his pervasiveness and is compassionate toward those who take refuge in him.
To the one who knows the essence,
to the one who knows the core.
Salutations for the support of all reality;
with one thousand and eight dark leaves of the *śrīphala* fruit, which possess the three principles (*tritatva*) and are of three kinds, may I worship [the goddess] Kalā...
